v1: Here's a question. You ask a chatbot the exact same thing twice. Do you get the same answer?
To find out, let's watch a language model write one sentence. It begins: the cat sat on the... and now it has to choose the next word.
It doesn't look anything up. Instead, it gives every word it knows a probability.
Mat is the most likely. Sofa and floor, less so. Moon, almost never. And all of the bars together always add up to one hundred percent.
Then it rolls a weighted die. Most of the time, the tallest bar wins. But not every time.
So the same question can come back with a different answer.
There's a dial for this, called temperature. Turn it down, and the top word takes over. Turn it up, and the bars even out, so surprising words show up more often.
Now the important part. Take the sentence: the capital of Australia is... Sydney gets a big share, because those words often appear together. But the capital is Canberra.
A model predicts likely words, and likely is not the same as true. Fluent answers still need checking. Try it yourself in the probability wheel lab.
v2: Imagine an app that spots pets in your photos. Its makers say it is ninety percent accurate. Sounds great. But accurate for whom?
Look at the photos it learned from. Almost all of them were taken in daylight. Only one in twenty was taken at night.
Next, we test it on the photos people really upload, where about a third are taken at night.
Overall, it scores about ninety percent. But let's split the results by group.
Day photos: ninety-seven percent. Night photos: about seventy-five. One night photo in four is wrong, and the average hid the gap.
Adding more daytime photos would not help. What helps is covering the missing group. So we make a quarter of the training photos night photos, and train again.
Now both groups are above ninety-five percent.

Real systems have shown the same pattern. Face analysis and speech recognition tools have worked far worse for people who were under-represented in their training data. So whenever you hear an accuracy number, ask: accurate for whom?
v3: An AI tool answers your question, and every sentence comes with a citation. Can you trust it?
Here is the answer, about the campus library on a Saturday. Instead of judging it as a whole, split it into claims, and check each one.
Claim one says the library opens at nine. Open the cited source and find the exact line. It says ten. Contradicted.
Second claim: show your student ID after eight. The source says exactly that. Supported.
The third claim cites section four point two of the access policy. But the policy only has three sections. That citation points at nothing. No real source.
Finally, claim four: study rooms can be booked a week ahead. Supported.
Two supported, one contradicted, and one invented. And all four had citations. A citation is a claim too.
So split the answer into claims, find each source yourself, confirm it says the same thing, then keep, fix, or drop. Practice in the claim-checking lab.
v4: You paste a draft into a chatbot and ask for feedback. Where does that text actually go?
Here's the prompt. Along with the essay, it includes a name, a student ID, and a health detail.
Every prompt is processed on the provider's servers. Depending on the settings, it may also be kept in your history, used to train future models, or shared with anyone who has a link.
With all of those switched on, three personal details are copied into four places. And deleting the chat from your list may not remove every copy.
Now the same request, done carefully. Remove what the task doesn't need, and turn off training and sharing where you can.
Same feedback on the essay, and no personal details anywhere.
Share only what the task needs, check each tool's settings, and prefer tools your university has approved. Try it yourself in the data trail lab.
v5: Quick test. Which of these is A I: a calculator, a spam filter, autocomplete, or an alarm clock?
A calculator follows fixed rules that a person wrote. Two plus two is four, every single time.
A spam filter is different. It learned from millions of emails that people marked as spam, and it keeps adjusting.
So here is the test: did the system learn its behavior from examples? Spam filter and autocomplete, yes. Calculator and alarm clock, no.
Every A I you use today is narrow A I. It is built for one kind of task. A model that writes fluent paragraphs cannot drive a car.
General A I, one system that could learn any task the way people do, is still a research goal. It is not what is on your phone.
So when a headline says an app understands everything, ask: what one task did it learn, and from what examples?
v6: Language models are very good at producing plausible language. Plausible is not the same as right.
Some tasks play to that strength: rewriting your own paragraph, summarizing a text you already have, brainstorming questions.
Notice what they share. You can judge the result yourself.
Other tasks are risky: exact numbers, recent events, and citations you have never seen.
Here the model may invent a source or a number, and say it with exactly the same confidence.
So before you use any output, ask one question: how would I know if this were wrong?
If you can check it easily, use it with care. If you cannot, treat it as a lead to verify, not as an answer.
v7: How does a model learn to spot a cat? Start with thousands of photos, each with a label: cat, dog, or no pet.
During training, the model adjusts millions of numbers until its guesses match the labels as often as possible.
It is not memorizing photos. It is finding patterns that separate cats from dogs.
To see whether it really learned, the team holds back labelled photos the model has never seen, and tests on those.
That is generalization: working on new examples. It works best on examples that look like the training data.
Show it a kind of photo it rarely saw, like one taken at night, and accuracy can drop sharply.
And remember: people chose what to collect, how to label it, and what got left out. Those choices decide who the model works for.
v8: An A I tool flags students as at risk. Before you trust it, ask five questions.
Who was it tested on? And how accurate is it for each group, not just overall?
What kinds of errors happen? Take an A I text detector.
A false positive says your own writing was made by A I. A false negative misses text that really was.
Detectors have been shown to flag writing by non-native English speakers more often. So the cost of false positives falls on some students more than others.
Then ask who pays for the errors, and who checks the decision. Real oversight means a person who can override the tool, and is accountable.
If you cannot find these answers, that is a finding too.
v9: Before you type anything into a chatbot, ask: what should I hand to A I at all?
Split the assignment. Support work: formatting references, checking grammar, organizing your notes.
Core work: forming the argument, analyzing the data, reflecting on your experience. That is the skill the assignment is building.
Delegate the core work, and the result may look good, but you skipped the learning.
Three questions before you delegate. Is this the skill I am meant to build? Is A I allowed here, and how? Can I check the result?
Whatever you delegate, you keep the final decision. You are responsible for what you submit.
Try it now: mark each part of your next assignment keep, delegate, or get feedback.
v10: Here is a weak request: explain the Calvin cycle. You will get a generic answer.
Add a goal: I am preparing for a biology quiz.
Add context: I understand the light reactions, but not the Calvin cycle.
Add constraints: plain language, under one hundred and fifty words, no skipped steps.
And add a format: end with three practice questions, with the answers at the bottom.
Now the model has a target it can hit, and you have something you can check against your textbook.
Then iterate. Ask which part it is least sure about, or ask it to quiz you.
v11: One course bans A I. Another requires it. A third allows it for some tasks. So what is the rule?
The rule is the policy of the course you are in. Find it in the syllabus or the assignment, and ask your instructor if it is unclear.
When A I is allowed, disclose it. Just saying I used A I tells your instructor almost nothing.
A good disclosure says three things: what tool, for what, and what you did with the output.
Keep a record of your key prompts, and of what you kept or changed.
Detectors make mistakes. If your work is questioned, your drafts and your record are the best evidence of your own process.
v12: You have learned how A I writes, who it works for, how to ask, and how to check. Now turn it into a plan.
First, the support tasks you will hand to A I, and the core skills you will keep for yourself.
Second, how you will ask: goal, context, constraints, and format.
Third, how you will check claims, sources and numbers, and what you will never share.
Fourth, a disclosure sentence you can adapt to each course.
Then revisit the plan after each big assignment. Did A I help where you expected? Did your checks catch anything?
Your plan will change as tools and policies change. That is what A I literacy looks like in practice.
